wave.in-november-2026-voters-propelled.html: In November 2026, voters propelled an unprecedented cohort of barrier-breaking leaders into statehouses, the Senate, Congress, and City Halls. This interactive intelligence grid transforms election outcomes into an accessible civic education tool.

wave.the-2026-midterms-swept-democrats.html: The 2026 midterms swept Democrats into power in states Trump carried easily, including Kansas, Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Ohio. The winners ran as pastors, loggers, pediatricians and teachers against corruption, billionaire money, the price of gas and groceries, and Big Tech’s data centers. This is the who, the why and the how, with the evidence and the places where the story is less tidy than it sounds.

wave.compared-with-trump-s-2024.html: Compared with Trump’s 2024 vote, Republican House candidates lost ground with nearly every group. The biggest swings came from Hispanic voters, independents and the young. The smallest came from white voters without a college degree, the core of the Republican base, which matters for how far “even conservatives” really goes.

wave.none-of-these-is-a.html: None of these is a culture-war issue. Each is about money, power or basic needs: what things cost, who gets rich from government, who controls the platforms and the power grid, whether you can see a doctor, and whether anyone checks the people at the top.

wave.across-very-different-states-and.html: Across very different states and ideologies, the winners repeated a handful of moves. Read these as patterns in the coverage, not a proven formula.

wave.the-wave-changed-who-holds.html: The wave changed who holds federal and state office. Much of daily life is still run by city councils, special districts, sheriffs and judges that few voters can name, and funded by money few can trace.

ledger.democrats-won-control-of-the.html: Democrats won control of the Senate and, on the AP tally, enough House seats for a majority, and at least 28 governorships. These counts are preliminary: two Senate races (Alaska, Mississippi) and two governor races (Alaska, Kansas) were uncalled on November 6.

ledger.five-prompts-for-working-through.html: Five prompts for working through what a “first” does and does not mean. Write your answers below each one; they stay in your browser and are not sent anywhere.

ledger.each-video-below-was-matched.html: Each video below was matched to its title and publishing channel on November 8, and each card has a transcript of its YouTube video: 15 were supplied by the site’s editor and 10 are YouTube’s own captions (3 uploaded by the publisher, 7 generated automatically). Transcripts were not proofread and may contain errors, so watch the video to verify. Quotes marked with a ▶ timestamp link to that moment in the video. Any quote without a timestamp comes from a news report and links to it. Six videos are not election-night speeches (two morning-after press conferences, interviews with supporters, two TV news reports, and a campaign speech from before the election), and each card says so. The transcripts and research notes are in the research folder. Videos load only when you press play, using YouTube’s privacy-enhanced mode.

ledger.channels-range-from-candidates-ow.html: Channels range from candidates’ own accounts to local TV stations and international outlets; a channel’s framing in a title is its own.

ledger.most-of-the-roughly-11.html: Most of the roughly 11,000 U.S. municipalities with 2,500 or more residents use one of two structures. Which one your city uses decides whether the mayor you elect runs anything, and who answers when a service fails.

ledger.share-of-10-969-municipalities.html: Share of 10,969 municipalities with 2,500+ residents, ICMA 2018.

ledger.the-often-repeated-line-that.html: The often-repeated line that council-manager cities are “nearly 10% more efficient” comes from a 2011 IBM benchmarking study of 100 large cities, not peer-reviewed research. ICMA reports that 66% of Moody’s Aaa-rated cities had a professional manager in 2016. Both are associations: well-off, stable cities may simply be more likely to choose professional management.

ledger.average-pay-for-a-full.html: Average pay for a full-time mayor (ICMA 2018).

ledger.average-pay-for-a-part.html: Average pay for a part-time mayor. Low pay narrows who can afford to serve.

ledger.share-of-city-council-seats.html: Share of city council seats held by women (ICMA 2018). 32% of cities elect some or all of their council by district.

ledger.ballotpedia-november-2026-at-the.html: Ballotpedia, November 2026. At the start of 2026, 81% of the top-100 population lived under a Democratic mayor; 22 of these seats were on the 2026 ballot.

ledger.term-limits-drove-much-of.html: Term limits drove much of the turnover. In Chandler, Irving, Knox County and Boca Raton the incumbent could not run, so the seat changed hands without any voter rejecting a sitting mayor. A change in a mayor’s party is not always a change in voters’ minds.

ledger.many-mayoral-races-are-officially.html: Many mayoral races are officially nonpartisan. Party labels do not appear on the ballot in Chandler, Irving or Los Angeles, so descriptions such as “Democratic gain” rely on candidates’ registrations or endorsements, which are not always public.

ledger.defeating-an-incumbent-is-rare.html: Defeating an incumbent is rare. Los Angeles was the exception: Karen Bass became the first sitting mayor there to lose since 2005, after the Palisades Fire and rising homelessness. Most incumbents on this list who ran were re-elected comfortably.

ledger.the-calendar-is-local-florida.html: The calendar is local. Florida cities often vote in March, Wisconsin in April, Texas in May and North Dakota in June. A common mistake is to assume every result came from November 3: this year’s mayoral races above were decided in March, April, June and August as well.

ledger.a-special-district-is-a.html: A special district is a separate local government created for one job: fire protection, water, sewers, libraries, hospitals, mosquito control. Many can levy property taxes and issue bonds, and each has its own board. The Census Bureau counted 39,555 in 2022, and 40,199 in its 2025 update, out of roughly 91,000 local governments. The commonly quoted “38,000” is the 2017 count.

ledger.the-tax-stack-over-one.html: The tax stack over one home

ledger.one-address-can-sit-inside.html: One address can sit inside a county, a city, a school district and several special districts, each taxing separately. The rates here are hypothetical and chosen only to show the structure; look up your own on your county assessor’s tax bill.

ledger.ask-yourself-how-many-of.html: Ask yourself: how many of these boards’ members could you name? How many of their elections did you vote in?

ledger.census-bureau-function-counts-202.html: Census Bureau function counts, 2022, grouped by this site. Total 39,555.

ledger.case-study-missoula-county-montan.html: Case study · Missoula County, Montana · February 2026

ledger.on-february-10-county-commissione.html: On February 10, county commissioners declared 12 special-district boards elected by acclamation because every candidate was unopposed, among them the Missoula Irrigation District. They cancelled elections in 15 more, including the Missoula Rural Fire District and the Turah Meadows Sewer and Water District, because nobody filed at all; those seats were opened for appointment. Local coverage shows the same thing happened in 2018, 2021, 2022 and 2025. It is routine, which is the point.

ledger.some-water-districts-limit-voting.html: Some water districts limit voting to landowners, weighted by acreage. The Supreme Court upheld this in Salyer Land Co. v. Tulare Lake Basin (1973) and Ball v. James (1981), reasoning that these districts serve land rather than people. It is one of the few places in American government where one person, one vote does not apply.

ledger.local-officials-control-zoning-bu.html: Local officials control zoning, building permits, public contracts and labor agreements, so the people affected by those decisions have reasons to fund local campaigns. But there is no national database of municipal campaign money. Any single national figure for “real estate’s share of local races” is a guess. The honest unit of analysis is one city at a time.

ledger.a-real-example-san-diego.html: A real example: San Diego City Council, 2022

ledger.maplight-common-cause-california-.html: MapLight / Common Cause California analysis of 2,678 individual donors.

ledger.796-donors-who-gave-the.html: 796 donors who gave the legal maximum, 30% of all donors, supplied about 67% of individual contributions. Real estate and construction interests gave about 17% of council campaign funding. Concentration, not a single industry, is the clearest pattern.

ledger.estimated-total-cost-of-the.html: Estimated total cost of the 2026 federal cycle, a record (OpenSecrets estimate, as reported by Al Jazeera).

ledger.outside-spending-from-just-five.html: Outside spending from just five groups by late October, per an AFP analysis of federal data, about a third of non-party outside spending.

ledger.the-united-states-is-unusual.html: The United States is unusual in electing many of the people who run its justice system: county sheriffs, district attorneys and, in most states, at least some judges. Election makes them answerable to voters. It also makes them answerable to whoever funds their campaigns.

ledger.hired-by-the-mayor-or.html: — Hired by the mayor or manager

ledger.about-78-of-people-held.html: About 78% of people held in U.S. jails in 2024 had not been convicted of the charge they were held on (Prison Policy Initiative, using federal data). Most pretrial detainees keep the right to vote, and the sheriff running their jail, the prosecutor and sometimes the judge may all be on their ballot.

ledger.there-is-no-national-figure.html: There is no national figure for how many actually vote. A court-ordered Massachusetts report released in June 2026 found 1% turnout among eligible people in jail in the 2024 primary and 5% in the general election. Harris County, Texas opened the state’s first jail polling place in November 2021.

ledger.how-states-choose-supreme-court.html: How states choose supreme court justices

ledger.initial-selection-method-all-50.html: Initial selection method, all 50 states (Ballotpedia). Kansas voters rejected a switch to elections on August 4, 2026.

ledger.assisted-appointment-often-called.html: Assisted appointment (often called the Missouri Plan): a commission screens candidates, the governor picks one, and the judge later faces a yes-or-no retention vote.

ledger.retention-elections-are-a-later.html: Retention elections are a later step, not a separate method, so a chart that counts them as a method alongside elections double-counts states.

ledger.in-ranked-choice-voting-also.html: In ranked choice voting (also called instant runoff), you rank candidates. If no one has more than half of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots move to each voter’s next choice still in the race. That repeats until someone has a majority of the ballots still counting. Washington, D.C. used it for the first time in June 2026.

ledger.16-jurisdictions-used-it-in.html: 16 jurisdictions used it in 2026, including Alaska, Maine, NYC and San Francisco.

ledger.irvine-ca-measure-leading-not.html: Irvine, CA measure leading, not yet called.

ledger.honolulu-rejected-it-44-6.html: Honolulu rejected it: 44.6% yes among votes cast on the question.

ledger.alaska-repeal-losing-on-election.html: Alaska repeal losing on election night with about 52% no; absentee ballots count for 15 days.

ledger.each-bloc-is-a-group.html: Each bloc is a group of voters who cast the same ranking. Drag a slider to change a bloc’s size, or change its rankings. Leave a choice blank to model voters who rank fewer candidates.

ledger.candidates-are-fictional-ties-for.html: Candidates are fictional. Ties for last place are broken by ballot order; real jurisdictions use lot or other statutory rules.
